title: ML storage hierarchy
question: Whose bandwidth is each storage tier sharing?
scope: Band widths show schematic capacity, not measured throughput; use the chapter table for quantities.

steps.title: Begin at HBM
steps.description: The top tier supplies one accelerator. Its bandwidth is not an aggregate shared-storage rating.

steps.title: Account for the node
steps.description: Host DRAM and local NVMe serve the accelerators inside one node. The bracket and eight-chip glyph identify the scope that must be divided among consumers.

steps.title: Divide shared supply
steps.description: Parallel file systems and object storage serve many nodes; archive is offline media. Growing the client fleet does not automatically increase this shared supply.

steps.title: Follow the physical route
steps.description: The right column progresses from an interposer to buses, networks, and offline media. A bandwidth comparison must retain both this route and its sharing scope.

title: Parallel file system architecture
question: How can a parallel file system separate lookup from bulk reads?
scope: The drawing is a Lustre-style logical architecture; aggregate OSS bandwidth is not a guarantee at any one client.

steps.title: Obtain the map
steps.description: Client 1 asks the metadata server for the stripe map stored on the metadata target. This lookup identifies the objects without sending the file payload through the MDS.

steps.title: Locate consecutive stripes
steps.description: Dark tiles 0, 1, 2, and N−1 occupy different OSTs. Each target also holds later stripes separated by N.

steps.title: Read in parallel
steps.description: The client uses the green data path to contact the OSS nodes directly. Multiple servers can supply different parts of the same file concurrently.

steps.title: Separate bottlenecks
steps.description: Every client shares the OSS service, while metadata stays on its own path. Adding data servers does not by itself increase metadata-operation capacity.

title: Measured Storage Demand per Accelerator
question: How does accelerator demand determine the storage bandwidth a fleet must deliver?
scope: MLPerf Storage uses emulated accelerators and fixed sample-consumption times. These passing submissions measure storage systems, not actual GPU execution.

steps.title: Scale the consumers
steps.description: The upper log-log plot shows throughput rising with the number of emulated accelerators. Each workload forms a different demand band.

steps.title: Compare sample workloads
steps.description: The lower bars show much higher per-accelerator demand for 3D U-Net than ResNet-50, with CosmoFlow between them. Data shape and consumption rate matter, not only accelerator count.

steps.title: Change the emulated generation
steps.description: Within each workload, the solid H100 bar exceeds the lighter A100 bar. Faster consumption raises required input bandwidth even when bytes per sample are unchanged.

steps.title: Size for the fleet workload
steps.description: A fleet’s required input rate combines consumer count with its workload-specific per-consumer demand. Passing busy-time thresholds define these observations, not unlimited storage scalability.

title: The data-stall frontier
question: When does more input bandwidth stop increasing ideal compute active time?
scope: The curve min(1, bandwidth/demand) is an ideal overlapped service-rate bound. Real utilization can lie below it because of latency, preparation, and coordination.

steps.title: Identify the service deficit
steps.description: Left of matching supply, the input stage cannot deliver batches as fast as compute consumes them. The stalled-notebook point sits at 0.8 ideal active fraction.

steps.title: Reach the knee
steps.description: At bandwidth/demand = 1, input supply matches consumption. The bound reaches active fraction 1 at this service-rate boundary.

steps.title: Interpret moderate headroom
steps.description: The image-job arrow spans 3.3 times matching bandwidth. It is supply margin, not a 3.3-times speedup above full compute activity.

steps.title: Interpret large headroom
steps.description: The text-job arrow spans 6,000 times demand while the bound remains flat. Additional input supply does not accelerate an already fed compute stage in this ideal model.

title: Pipelined data loading
question: What work must overlap to keep a GPU supplied with batches?
scope: Equal timeline scales and durations are illustrative. Successful overlap requires sufficient delivery rate and prefetch depth.

steps.title: Find avoidable idle time
steps.description: In panel a, GPU idle intervals cover storage reads and CPU preparation. One batch finishes before the next begins its input work.

steps.title: Overlap different batches
steps.description: Panel b prepares future batches while the GPU trains on an earlier batch. Read, preparation, and training are concurrent work on different resources.

steps.title: Inspect one instant
steps.description: The shaded column crosses read 4, prep 3, and train 2. Three batches need distinct in-flight state; this overlap is not three operations on one batch.

steps.title: Check sustained delivery
steps.description: Back-to-back training blocks follow the initial fill. They remain possible only while input stages keep up and buffering absorbs variability.

title: Traditional vs. GPUDirect Storage path
question: Which bytes and control operations does GPUDirect Storage change?
scope: Panel a is the particular buffered baseline drawn, not every conventional I/O configuration. Routes encode payload paths, not transfer timing.

buffer.label: Host bounce buffers and CPU copy

steps.title: Stage the buffered payload
steps.description: DMA 1 brings NVMe payload into the kernel buffer in host DRAM. The CPU copies it to a pinned buffer before the next DMA.

steps.title: Reach the GPU
steps.description: DMA 2 transfers the pinned payload into GPU HBM. Both green hops carry payload through the same PCIe switching fabric.

steps.title: Bypass host payload storage
steps.description: The GDS panel routes NVMe payload directly to GPU HBM. Removing the host bounce stage changes byte movement.

steps.title: Retain orchestration
steps.description: The dashed CPU control link still submits and completes I/O. A direct payload path does not mean the host and software control path disappear.

title: The complete data path
question: Which data copies must the training loop wait for?
scope: This running example bypasses the parallel file system for training input; other deployments can stage differently.

input.label: Prefetch, batch, and optional GDS path

steps.title: Stage the input once
steps.description: The dashed arrow copies the dataset from object storage into local NVMe. This once-per-job work differs from a transfer required for every training batch.

steps.title: Supply each batch
steps.description: Solid arrows move staged input through host prefetch to GPU HBM. The optional GDS route bypasses host DRAM for payload movement.

steps.title: Pause for a local save
steps.description: Checkpoint traffic starts at model state in HBM and writes a local shard. That solid path is inside the GPU node and is part of the training pause.

steps.title: Make the save durable
steps.description: Dashed copies carry shards to the parallel file system and selected checkpoints to object storage. Background copying needs a completed durable generation before it becomes a restore point.

title: The memory wall
question: Why must frontier training state extend beyond one accelerator?
scope: The model-demand series uses 16 bytes per parameter for mixed-precision Adam. Plotted frontier models are selected examples; GPT-3 is the first crossing among those points, not the first partitioned model in history.

steps.title: Read capacity as one device
steps.description: The blue capacity series describes individual accelerators, not total fleet memory. Its growth is substantial but remains far below later training-state demand.

steps.title: Include complete training state
steps.description: The red series includes weights, gradients, and optimizer state under the stated 16-byte convention. A parameter-only estimate would be a different quantity.

steps.title: Inspect the plotted crossing
steps.description: GPT-3 is the first shown model beyond one accelerator, by roughly 35 times the largest device of its year. Models between the plotted points can already have required partitioning.

steps.title: Treat sharding as feasibility
steps.description: PaLM and Llama 3 remain far above the capacity curve. For these examples, spreading training state across devices is needed to fit before it can improve speed.

title: The 3D parallelism cube
question: Which training relationship does each axis of the device cube represent?
scope: The cube is a configuration schematic. Memory fit, divisibility, and network placement must still be checked.

steps.title: Split a layer
steps.description: The horizontal tensor axis groups devices that shard work within a layer. Its communication is frequent enough that placement within a fast domain matters.

steps.title: Place sequential stages
steps.description: The vertical pipeline axis separates layers into stages that exchange activations and gradients. It changes where a batch executes through depth.

steps.title: Replicate for batches
steps.description: The diagonal data axis groups replicas processing different batch shards. These ranks exchange model-update information.

steps.title: Count the combined configuration
steps.description: The printed product multiplies all three degrees to give device count. Increasing an axis changes its own traffic and per-device state, not just the total number of GPUs.

title: Data parallelism implementation pipeline
question: Why do independent replicas finish with identical parameter updates?
scope: The diagram describes the shown averaged-gradient SGD workflow; preserving global-batch semantics depends on matching batch and averaging conventions.

steps.title: Partition the global batch
steps.description: The batch of 128 examples becomes four shards of 32 in this illustrated case. Each GPU receives different examples while starting from the same model state.

steps.title: Compute local gradients
steps.description: Each replica performs forward and backward work independently and produces its own gradient gᵢ. Local data differences make those gradients different.

steps.title: Average across replicas
steps.description: AllReduce combines all local gradients into one global average. This collective synchronizes the update information, rather than sending examples through the GPUs in sequence.

steps.title: Apply the same update
steps.description: Every GPU applies the common averaged gradient and reaches the same updated parameters. Replica agreement is what permits the next global-batch step.

title: Communication patterns and their costs
question: How do aggregation and peer routing stress the network differently?
scope: Volumes shown use the diagram’s simplified communication model; the All-to-All graph gives logical destinations rather than physical cables.

steps.title: Spread aggregation traffic
steps.description: Ring AllReduce exchanges with neighbors and spreads traffic over ring links. The footer gives per-GPU volume under the displayed model.

steps.title: Inspect the shared ingress
steps.description: Workers send and receive through the parameter server NIC. The red central segment identifies a shared aggregation bottleneck.

steps.title: Route distinct payloads
steps.description: Logical All-to-All sends different data to each peer. A switched fabric can realize these destinations; routes, message sizes, and contention determine the cost.

title: Distributed synchronization models
question: What does relaxing a global barrier permit workers to do?
scope: The timelines are schematic; removing a global barrier does not eliminate resource contention or guarantee better convergence.

steps.title: Wait at every barrier
steps.description: BSP holds workers at each step boundary until the slow worker arrives. Hatched waits accumulate even on workers that finished their compute.

steps.title: Permit a bounded lead
steps.description: SSP allows workers to move ahead only within its staleness bound. Faster workers eventually wait when that allowance is exhausted.

steps.title: Remove the global barrier
steps.description: ASP lets workers advance without a global update barrier. Their progress diverges, so updates may use stale state; communication and contention still impose delays.

title: ZeRO memory reduction
question: Which persistent state term makes early ZeRO stages effective?
scope: The example is a 7B-parameter model on 64 ranks at 16 bytes per parameter. Bars exclude activations, temporary gathered parameters, communication buffers, and runtime allocations.

steps.title: Find the largest replicated term
steps.description: DDP stores 14 GB weights, 14 GB gradients, and 84 GB optimizer state per rank. The 112 GB stack exceeds the displayed 80 GB ceiling.

steps.title: Shard optimizer state first
steps.description: ZeRO-1 retains replicated weights and gradients while partitioning the largest term. The remaining 29.3 GB persistent stack already fits below that ceiling.

steps.title: Continue partitioning
steps.description: ZeRO-2 also shards gradients; ZeRO-3 also shards parameters. The bars shrink to 15.5 GB and 1.75 GB under this fixed example.

steps.title: Check the actual peak separately
steps.description: Dashed outlines mark removed replicated state, not extra free capacity guaranteed to a batch. Activations and transient gathered state must still fit simultaneously.

title: ZeRO state partitioning across GPU ranks
question: Which training-state copies disappear at each ZeRO stage?
scope: Four ranks and 2/2/12 bytes per parameter are the diagram’s mixed-precision Adam example; tile width is a shard fraction, not actual relative byte size.

steps.title: Identify replicated ownership
steps.description: In DDP every rank holds complete W, G, and O tiles. Rank count therefore does not reduce each rank’s persistent model-state footprint.

steps.title: Shard optimizer state
steps.description: ZeRO-1 distributes O across ranks. Quarter-width filled segments show different owners while W and G remain replicated.

steps.title: Also shard gradients
steps.description: ZeRO-2 distributes both G and O. Dashed outlines mark the full stacks each rank no longer stores persistently.

steps.title: Shard weights and communicate
steps.description: ZeRO-3 also distributes W. Its footer records higher per-worker communication because parameters must be gathered when needed.

title: The scaling tax
question: Why can a small residual baseline fraction cap a large fleet’s speedup?
scope: These curves use fixed illustrative residual fractions in N/(1+(N−1)r). Actual communication and coordination can change with device count; r is not the profiler’s distributed-step synchronization share.

steps.title: Begin near the linear regime
steps.description: At small N, the curves lie close together because the unscaled residual has not yet overtaken the divided compute term.

steps.title: Keep a tiny residual visible
steps.description: Even the 0.1 percent curve falls below the ideal diagonal at large N. A small baseline fraction can matter once compute is divided over many devices.

steps.title: Inspect the asymptote
steps.description: The 1 percent curve bends toward 1/r = 100. Adding GPUs cannot remove a residual that this model leaves fixed.

steps.title: Recognize an early ceiling
steps.description: At 10 percent the total speedup approaches ten despite hundreds of GPUs. This is a model sensitivity result, not a measured limit for a particular collective.

title: Measured Scaling in MLPerf Training
question: What can measured time-to-quality scaling reveal—and leave unresolved?
scope: Each series compares one benchmark round and configuration family. Larger global batches can alter convergence, so deviation from ideal is not entirely communication overhead.

steps.title: Compare within a series
steps.description: Color and legend identify five benchmark/configuration series. Their smallest runs establish separate baselines; this is not a controlled cross-hardware contest.

steps.title: Read the ideal reference
steps.description: Dashed lines divide each baseline time by its scale increase. They define perfect relative scaling from that series’ smallest configuration.

steps.title: Inspect retained efficiency
steps.description: The largest configurations finish faster but lie above their ideal lines. The printed 71–84 percent labels quantify retained relative scaling for these runs.

steps.title: Separate time and convergence
steps.description: Time-to-quality includes both step execution and the number of steps or examples required. Batch-dependent convergence must be inspected before attributing the whole gap to the fabric.

title: Statistical cost of larger batches
question: Why can fewer optimizer steps still require more total examples?
scope: This normalized gradient-noise illustration uses a fitted critical batch B*. It is not a hardware-throughput optimum or a measured threshold for a specific model.

steps.title: Increase a small batch
steps.description: Below B*, the blue optimization-step curve falls almost inversely with batch size while the orange example count stays near its minimum.

steps.title: Reach the statistical crossover
steps.description: At B/B* = 1 both normalized costs equal 2. The intersection describes a trade-off in this model, not the fastest hardware operating point.

steps.title: Observe diminishing step savings
steps.description: Above the crossover, blue steps flatten toward their lower limit. Further batch growth buys progressively less reduction in optimizer updates.

steps.title: Pay for extra samples
steps.description: The orange examples curve continues upward even as steps flatten. Device throughput and convergence must both enter the time-to-quality decision.

title: Cost and time in the illustrative scaling scenario
question: Which configuration is dominated in this cost–time scenario?

steps.title: Choose the lower bill
steps.description: Eight-worker BSP is the lower-cost point, but it sits much farther right on the logarithmic time axis. Lower cost comes with a later result.

steps.title: Buy a faster result

steps.title: Account for convergence
steps.description: The assumed SSP run is both slower and more expensive than 64-worker BSP. Its per-step savings are outweighed by additional iterations in this scenario.

steps.title: Use the domination test narrowly
steps.description: The shaded region is worse in both axes than an available BSP run. This is a scenario-specific frontier, not a general rejection of asynchronous designs.

title: Layer-wise model parallelism
question: Why is splitting layers alone insufficient to keep all GPUs busy?
scope: Sixteen layers, four GPUs, and equal schematic slots form the worked case; the schedule contains one batch without microbatching.

steps.title: Reduce each weight footprint
steps.description: Four consecutive layers occupy each GPU. Forward activations move right and backward gradients move left across stage boundaries.

steps.title: Follow one batch forward
steps.description: Only one stage handles this batch’s forward work in a slot. The other GPUs cannot invent later-stage input before its dependency arrives.

steps.title: Return gradients in reverse
steps.description: Backward work starts at the final stage and returns toward GPU 0. The reverse dependency leaves most stages idle again.

steps.title: Count utilization in this schedule
steps.description: Each GPU is busy for two of eight slots in this simplified schedule. Microbatching can fill some of the remaining slots with other batches’ work.

title: Pipeline parallelism schedule
question: Where do fill and drain bubbles remain in a microbatched pipeline?
scope: This is GPipe-style all-forward-then-all-backward scheduling with four stages, four microbatches, and equal illustrative slots.

steps.title: Fill the pipeline
steps.description: Early stages start microbatches before later stages have inputs. The left hatched triangles are dependency-driven idle slots.

steps.title: Keep multiple batches active
steps.description: Forward blocks m1 through m4 form a diagonal wave. Different stages can work concurrently because they hold different microbatches.

steps.title: Respect backward dependencies
steps.description: Backward blocks return in reverse microbatch order. A stage waits for the next stage’s gradient for that same microbatch.

steps.title: Retain the bubble cost
steps.description: The summary shows six of fourteen slots idle for every stage. Microbatching improves occupancy here but does not remove fill and drain.

title: Matrix partitioning under tensor parallelism
question: Why can one tensor-parallel layer pair communicate only after partial sums?
scope: The figure illustrates the displayed Megatron-style layer pair on two GPUs; it is not a communication bound for every model layer.

column.label: Replicated X and column shards A₁/A₂

local.label: Local Y slices and row shards B₁/B₂

steps.title: Split output columns
steps.description: Both GPUs read replicated X but use different column shards of A. Each produces its own Y slice.

steps.title: Consume matching slices locally
steps.description: The following row-parallel B shard consumes its matching Y slice on the same GPU. The marked no-communication boundary preserves this pairing.

steps.title: Sum partial results
steps.description: Z₁ and Z₂ are partial contributions to the same output, not independent complete outputs. AllReduce sums them.

steps.title: Recover a replicated output
steps.description: Both GPUs receive full Z after the collective. This is where the displayed pair restores the result needed by the next operation.

title: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) AllToAll routing
question: Why does expert execution require two peer exchanges?
scope: The artwork traces token a with top-1 routing across four ranks, one expert per rank. The general gate may choose more experts.

steps.title: Choose an expert
steps.description: Token a begins on rank 0 but its gate selects Expert 2. Input ownership and expert placement need not match.

steps.title: Dispatch to expert owners
steps.description: The first All-to-All sends token payloads to their selected experts. Highlighted token a crosses from rank 0 to Expert 2.

steps.title: Execute the expert
steps.description: Each expert runs its FFN on the routed tokens it receives, which may originate from multiple ranks. Uneven routing can also produce unequal loads.

steps.title: Return and combine
steps.description: The second exchange returns expert results to original token owners. Rank 0 combines the result for a with its gate weight, preserving the source token order.

title: One PPO-style RLHF step
question: Which models in a PPO-style RLHF step need optimizer state?
scope: The diagram is one PPO-style arrangement. State strip widths follow 2/2/12 bytes per parameter and are not the equal-width ZeRO columns.

steps.title: Generate responses

steps.title: Run frozen evaluators

title: Parallelism strategy decision framework
question: Which constraint should determine the first parallelism candidate?
scope: This is a selection guide, not an automatic optimizer. Peak memory, global batch, input delivery, bandwidth, and imbalance constrain every branch.

steps.title: Start with memory fit
steps.description: A model that fits on one GPU can remain single-device if it meets the target. Otherwise data parallelism is a candidate, provided input delivery and global-batch constraints permit it.

steps.title: Identify what breaks the budget
steps.description: A deep sequence of layers suggests pipeline stages. A single oversized layer suggests tensor partitioning rather than only moving whole layers.

steps.title: Consider state sharding
steps.description: The remaining memory case leads to sharded data parallelism such as FSDP or ZeRO. The candidate cards describe different state and communication arrangements.

steps.title: Combine after checking constraints
steps.description: The bottom box combines TP, PP, and DP when necessary. The guide does not remove the need to validate memory peaks and the network hierarchy.

title: The N-models complexity explosion
question: Why can portfolio coordination outgrow per-model monitoring work?
scope: All growth shapes and team capacity are illustrative. The near-50 crossing is not a measured staffing threshold or a scheduling complexity theorem.

steps.title: Separate fixed work per model
steps.description: The dotted blue alert curve grows linearly with model count under the assumed fixed monitoring burden per model.

steps.title: Include coordination work
steps.description: Deployment coordination grows as the assumed N log N sketch. Release dependencies can add work beyond simply operating each model independently.

steps.title: Inspect dense dependency risk
steps.description: The purple curve reflects a dense-pair quadratic assumption. A real registry’s recorded edge density determines which model pairs can actually conflict.

steps.title: Measure before choosing the threshold
steps.description: The total crosses the illustrative team-capacity line near 50 models. A platform decision needs measured repeated work and remediation costs, not this count alone.

title: The platform benefit-cost threshold
question: How does a benefit–cost ratio differ from net ROI?
scope: The model assumes $100K annual benefit per model and fixed $2M/year or $5M/year running cost. These are not the separate worked example’s one-time build costs.

steps.title: Locate annual break-even
steps.description: The horizontal line at benefit/cost = 1 means annual benefit equals annual running cost. Net ROI is zero there, not 100 percent.

steps.title: Change the cost budget
steps.description: With the fixed per-model benefit, the $2M/year platform crosses at 20 models and the $5M/year platform at 50. Higher fixed annual cost requires more benefit to cover it.

steps.title: Translate the ratio
steps.description: At 100 models the cheaper platform has benefit/cost = 5. Subtracting the original cost gives net ROI = 4, or 400 percent.

steps.title: Preserve the assumptions
steps.description: The straight lines assume constant marginal benefit and fixed platform cost. Dependency growth or diminishing savings would change the slopes and crossings.

title: Dependency-aware model registry
question: How far can a registry safely propagate a model change?
scope: Only recorded dependency edges are traversed. The drawing omits direct embedding-to-ranker feature edges described in the caption.

steps.title: Start at the changed artifact
steps.description: Embedding E moves from v3.1 to v3.2. The registry starts from this versioned artifact and follows its recorded downstream edges.

steps.title: Expand the impact set
steps.description: Retrieval R and rankers K₁ through K₃ are downstream of the change. Re-evaluation includes consumers beyond the directly connected retrieval node.

steps.title: Reach the final consumer

steps.title: Inspect the blind spot
steps.description: Fraud model F is not flagged because its edge is unrecorded. An empty registry edge is not proof of independence.

title: E-commerce model ecosystem
question: Why does an embedding change require coordinated evaluation?
scope: The graph gives declared data dependencies, not measured effect sizes; a dependency identifies evaluation scope rather than proving a regression.

steps.title: Build two representations
